fetched_contents.text: Stabilisation of waterlogged archaeological wood: the analysis of structural and dimensional changes of different conservation methods using magnetic resonance imaging and X-ray micro-computed tomography Abstract Waterlogged archaeological wood can be preserved for many years in the absence of air, as decomposition is substantially slowed down. After excavation, conservation is necessary to prevent damage of objects due to uncontrolled drying. In this study, the following conservation methods were tested to investigate their ability to stabilise the objects: alcohol-ether resin, melamine-formaldehyde (Kauramin 800), lactitol/trehalose, saccharose, polyethylene glycol (PEG 2000 with air-drying and PEG 2000 or 400 and 4000 with subsequent freeze-drying). In order to precisely understand the changes caused by conservation and drying, 40 samples each of pine wood and oak wood were documented using magnetic resonance imaging and X-ray micro-computed tomography before and after conservation. This imaging made it possible to quantitatively record changes in the wood structure, for example due to shrinkage, collapse and cracks, which could not be prevented by conservation. The alcohol-ether-resin method with solvent drying had the best stabilizing effect and no damage of the wood structure was visible. The two PEG treatments followed by freeze drying showed effective volume stabilisation. In both cases, however, the treatment led to cracks in the wood structure, which occurred less frequently when the cryoprotectant PEG 400 was used. In comparison, the other methods with air drying did not show consistently good results in stabilizing the volume or wood structure. Keywords: Conservation, Waterlogged archaeological wood, Collapse, Cracks, Volume, Shrinkage, X-ray micro-computed tomography, Magnetic resonance imaging Subject terms: Engineering, Materials science Introduction Wood can be preserved in temperate climate zones in water bodies or water-saturated soils under anoxic conditions over a very long period of time. The degradation of wood under such conditions takes place very slowly and leads to a change in the structure and composition of the objects: Primarily, the cellulose components of the secondary cell wall are decomposed by microorganisms such as fungi (soft-rot fungi (SR)) and bacteria (tunnelling bacteria (TB) and erosion bacteria (EB))1. Furthermore, lignin can be degraded by oxidation and hydrolysis2. This degradation is a common process that leads to decay of the wood, in which ultimately only the skeletal framework of the middle lamella holds the structure together. The secondary cell wall, which is primarily responsible for the stability of the undamaged wood3, then contains only degraded lignin and bacterial slime4. The process can be very heterogeneous and some cells can be degraded while neighbouring cells remain undamaged5. This decomposition, which begins in the outer regions, leads to physical weakening of the structure and to fragility of the archaeological wood during ground deposition6. Water from the environment fills the pore spaces - the capillaries and microcapillaries - and causes the wood structure to swell. Waterlogged archaeological wood (WAW) continues to decompose, and the interaction of microorganisms, fungal attack and chemical reactions with salt and fresh water can increase this decomposition and lead to extensive damage that compromises the structural integrity of the wood remains7. The more cell wall material is broken down, the more water fills the internal cavities. The maximum water content therefore increases as the wood degrades and is an universally used indicator of the state of preservation8. WAW is very sensitive after excavation and can suffer considerable damage within a few hours without protective measures. Due to the increased oxygen supply after excavation, WAW is also susceptible to degradation by oxygen-tolerant microorganisms1 and other oxygen-related degradation processes. If WAW air-dries, capillary forces occur due to the high surface tension of the evaporating water. This causes the cell walls to shrink and the cells to collapse9,10. Depending on the degree of degradation, only a fraction of the wood volume remains. The dimensional changes during drying happen in two stages11: Above the fibre saturation point, degraded cells collapse due to capillary tension and drying stress12,13. Below the fibre saturation point, the cell walls begin to shrink, whereby the volume loss of WAW is proportional to the water content and the shrinkage in tangential direction is generally greater than in radial and longitudinal direction10. Wood has unique material properties and is also readily available and easy to work with. Due to its frequent use and the information stored in wood anatomy, it plays an irreplaceable role in the study of the way of life of people and their environment in the past. This requires the permanent preservation of these unique sources, which has led to the development of methods to prevent uncontrolled drying out14. The damaging effect of air-drying and the question of how to solve this problem was recognized as early as the 19th century as not an easy task15, and since that time a variety of methods and conservation agents have been tested14. Currently there are two different strategies to preserve WAW: the (re-) burial in a protected, natural, anaerobic and waterlogged environment and conservation treatments. To avoid shrinkage, rupture, splits, cracks and collapse of WAW upon drying is the main challenge for the conservation16. In addition to the preservation of cultural heritage, conservation measures are required to minimise the impact on the material properties for possible future investigations17. fetched_contents.text: Quantitative Analysis of Electron Beam Damage in Organic Thin Films Abstract In transmission electron microscopy (TEM) the interaction of an electron beam with polymers such as P3HT:PCBM photovoltaic nanocomposites results in electron beam damage, which is the most important factor limiting acquisition of structural or chemical data at high spatial resolution. Beam effects can vary depending on parameters such as electron dose rate, temperature during imaging, and the presence of water and oxygen in the sample. Furthermore, beam damage will occur at different length scales. To assess beam damage at the angstrom scale, we followed the intensity of P3HT and PCBM diffraction rings as a function of accumulated electron dose by acquiring dose series and varying the electron dose rate, sample preparation, and the temperature during acquisition. From this, we calculated a critical dose for diffraction experiments. In imaging mode, thin film deformation was assessed using the normalized cross-correlation coefficient, while mass loss was determined via changes in average intensity and standard deviation, also varying electron dose rate, sample preparation, and temperature during acquisition. The understanding of beam damage and the determination of critical electron doses provides a framework for future experiments to maximize the information content during the acquisition of images and diffraction patterns with (cryogenic) transmission electron microscopy. Introduction Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) is one of the main tools to investigate the morphology of materials, from subnanometer to micrometer length scales. However, the interaction of electrons with materials, and especially beam sensitive structures such as polymers,1 biological materials,2,3 or zeolites,4 causes different types of radiation damage, e.g., atomic displacement, electrostatic charging, sputtering, radiolysis, and knock-on damage.5 These mechanisms operate at different length scales: At subnanometer length scales, knock-on damage and atomic displacement can result in distorted crystal lattices, while morphology changes due to heating, electrostatic charging and sputtering are visible at nanometer and micrometer length scales. Hence, for beam sensitive materials, beam damage constitutes a physical limit and determines the resolution that can be achieved in imaging, diffraction, and electron tomography.6 Therefore, it is important to analyze and understand beam damage to facilitate the study of these (beam sensitive) materials with a minimum amount of artifacts. The degradation of crystal lattices, at subnanometer length scales, can be studied by electron diffraction. It is well established that electron beam damage causes the fading of diffraction spots and rings in protein crystallography,7 and it has been shown that it is affected by the temperature of the material, the electron flux through the material, and the accumulated amount of electrons transmitting the material.8−15 Furthermore, this effect is easily quantified by following the intensity of diffraction rings or spots as a function of accumulated dose.9,16−20 The effects of beam damage at nanometer and micrometer length scales are dependent on and specific to the utilized imaging mode but mainly relate to materials loss by sputtering, and shrinkage.21−24 The degradation of materials causes artifacts in the form of changes in contrast or local intensity, while mass loss will result in an increase in overall intensity.25 In the literature, this phenomenon is mostly studied by using the difference image of two images with different accumulated electron doses.26,27 These techniques, however, is not commonly used to follow beam damage over a multitude of images,25 which is essential for e.g. electron tomography.24,28 The analysis of organic photovoltaics (OPVs) is a good example where beam sensitivity plays an important part.28 OPVs contain a photoactive layer, which is composed of different organic molecules. Since the morphology of this photoactive layer, i.e., the distribution of molecules, including their nanoscale phase separation, has a large impact on the overall efficiency of OPVs, TEM has become a standard characterization tool. Common OPV materials are e.g. poly(3-hexylthiophene) (P3HT) and phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM). These materials show diffraction rings instead of diffraction spots, resulting from the random orientation of crystallites or the presence of amorphous phases. Therefore, radial averaging of diffraction patterns is a suitable way to record and analyze the intensity change of P3HT and PCBM diffraction signals29 upon electron beam damage. In the analysis of OPVs, TEM samples are usually created by floating the photoactive layer on water from a water-soluble polymer film.30 The resulting water that is present in the sample might play a role in beam damage mechanisms as well, for example, by creating oxygen radicals. An oxygen- and water-free sample preparation method is therefore introduced to specifically study the influence of sample preparation. In this paper, beam damage is studied in both diffraction and bright field imaging, investigating the effect of electron dose rate, temperature, and sample preparation. More specifically, (1) beam damage of the crystallinity is quantified via radially averaged diffraction patterns, (2) mass loss is assessed via changes in intensity and standard deviation of the mean intensity, and (3) shrinkage is determined by monitoring the movement of markers, while a method is introduced to determine shrinkage or expansion via the use of the normalized cross-correlation. fetched_contents.text: Methyltrimethoxysilane as a stabilising agent for archaeological waterlogged wood differing in the degree of degradation Introduction Conservation of historic wood aims at enhancing various wood properties such as durability (in terms of resistance to biological degradation), moisture sorption, strength, hardness, fire endurance and preservation of its original appearance. Moreover, if the conserved wooden object is planned to be exposed outside, the conservation process should also impart wood stability towards UV-radiation and improvement of its weathering performance. However, in the case of waterlogged wood which is saturated with water and often severely degraded, the first and most important step is to consolidate its structure and maintain its original shape and dimensions. Decomposed and deprived of the texture strengthening cellulose, wooden cell walls weaken and tend to collapse during wood drying (e.g. [1], [2], [3]). Therefore, in order to effectively reinforce its internal structure and protect it against irreversible cracking, shrinkage and disintegration, wet archaeological wood requires appropriate methods of conserving treatment. Owing to the fact that waterlogged wood differs considerably depending on the species, degree and type of degradation, permeability, growth anomalies, and history of use, it is impossible to apply one versatile treatment. Therefore, various types of chemical compounds and methods have been used so far for its conservation and consolidation, taking into account also budget and traditions within different conservation professions. These include several types of treatment, such as impregnation and bulking, polar solvent drying, slow air-drying, freeze-drying, and in situ polymerisation [4]. Impregnation and bulking encompasses historical alum treatment using different alum salt concentrations and a mixture thereof with additional compounds, such as glycerol [5], [6], application of a wide range of carbohydrates or sugar alcohols (e.g. sucrose [7], lactitol [8], [9], trehalose and sucralose [10], and proteins (e.g. hydrolysed feather keratin [11], [12]). Various resins have also been used, e.g. colophony (rosin), esterified colophonies and vinyl acetate for impregnation of acetone-dehydrated wood [13], [14], melamine formaldehyde resin or glycol methacrylate [15], as well as waxes [16]. However, definitely the most common consolidant is still polyethylene glycol (PEG). It has been used in a wide range of molecular weights for one- or two-step wood treatment (soaking or spraying), with or without freeze-drying [e.g. [15], [17]. The treatment takes time and full impregnation results in a heavy weight of the treated object as well as an unnaturally dark colour of wood with a shiny, waxy finish of PEG on its surface [4], [18]. Branch report on sample preparation limitations

Sample preparation for SEM of degraded archaeological wood is limited by the same drying and embalming processes that are needed for conservation, because those processes can alter cell structure and cause collapse. The evidence shows that waterlogged archaeological wood is preserved for many years in the absence of air, but uncontrolled drying after excavation accelerates deterioration and can cause shrinkage, collapse, cracks, and loss of structure [N4-F2]. It also explains that wood dehydration prior to treatment is the key factor for effective cell wall bulking by silane monomers, reinforcing the structure and improving dimensional stability, but that dehydration can still cause collapse and cracking if not carefully managed [N1-R5]. A waterlogged wood conservation review emphasizes that wood can collapse during drying, especially when it is already severely degraded, and that shrinkage and collapse are major problems for conservation [N4-R3]. This means that preparation-induced drying can distort the original cell structure rather than preserving it intact.

A second major limitation is mechanical handling and fragmentation, which can distort interpretation and lose context. The conservation evidence notes that waterlogged wood is very sensitive after excavation and can suffer considerable damage within a few hours without protective measures, and that uncontrolled drying can lead to shrinkage, rupture, splits, cracks, and collapse [N4-F2]. It also says that the structural and dimensional changes caused by conservation can include shrinkage, cracks, and volume loss, and that the more cell wall material is broken down, the more water fills the internal cavities [N1-F1]. This suggests that any handling or sectioning required for SEM can further fragment the sample and erase the spatial relationships that are important for interpreting degradation history. The evidence does not explicitly mention fragmentation as a separate artifact, but the repeated emphasis on collapse, cracks, and loss of structure implies that mechanical stress during sample preparation can distort the sample and reduce the representativeness of the SEM view.

A third limitation is coating and conductive treatment, which can obscure morphology or create artifacts. The SEM preparation evidence explains that conductive coatings are commonly applied to insulating or beam-sensitive materials to reduce electric charge buildup on the sample surface [N2-R3]. It also says that gold or platinum coating is used to reduce the charge that builds up on insulating samples, enabling sharp, high-resolution imaging [N2-R1][N2-R2]. While these treatments are standard for SEM, they can obscure morphology or create artifacts because they add a layer that is not part of the original material. The evidence does not provide direct SEM-specific examples of wood artifacts from coating, but it does support the general principle that conductive treatment can affect imaging quality and that such coatings are needed only when the sample is non-conductive [N2-R3]. In the context of fragile archaeological wood, this means that the addition of a conductive layer may be necessary to avoid charging artifacts, but it also risks introducing a separate layer that can obscure fine structure or create a false impression of the material’s native state.

Overall, the main sample-preparation limitations are: drying and dehydration can cause collapse, cracks, and structural loss; mechanical handling can fragment and distort the sample; and conductive coatings can obscure morphology or create artifacts [N4-F2][N1-R5][N2-R3].

Branch report on archaeological wood-specific preservation issues

Waterlogged and degraded wood undergoes collapse, delamination, and resin loss as part of its preservation history. The conservation evidence states that waterlogged archaeological wood can be preserved for many years in the absence of air because decomposition is substantially slowed down, but that once excavation begins, conservation is necessary to prevent damage from uncontrolled drying [N4-F2]. It also explains that waterlogged wood is sensitive after excavation and can suffer considerable damage within a few hours without protective measures, and that uncontrolled drying can lead to shrinkage, rupture, splits, cracks, and collapse [N4-F2]. The same source describes how the more cell wall material is broken down, the more water fills the internal cavities, and that the process can be heterogeneous, with some cells degraded while neighboring cells remain undamaged [N1-F1]. This heterogeneity implies that resin loss and delamination are likely to occur in the same sample, because degradation can be uneven and structural integrity can be lost in parts of the wood even when other parts are still intact [N1-F1][N4-F2].

Preservation history and post-depositional alteration complicate interpretation because the sample is already damaged before it is examined. The evidence notes that waterlogged wood can be preserved for many years in anaerobic conditions, but after excavation, conservation becomes necessary because the wood is vulnerable to decomposition, oxygen-tolerant microorganisms, and other post-depositional alteration processes [N4-F2]. The review also says that the degradation of wood under such conditions changes the structure and composition of the objects, and that the secondary cell wall, which is primarily responsible for the stability of undamaged wood, then contains only degraded lignin and bacterial slime [N1-F1]. This means that the SEM view is not a pristine snapshot of the original wood; it is a sample that has already undergone complex post-depositional changes, including microbial attack, chemical degradation, and physical weakening [N1-F2][N4-F2]. That makes it difficult to distinguish between original anatomical features and later damage.

Sample size, orientation, and sectioning affect the representativeness of the SEM view because smaller or cut samples may miss important structural features and context. The conservation evidence emphasizes that waterlogged wood can be preserved for many years in water-saturated conditions, but that conservation is needed to prevent damage during drying [N4-F2]. It also notes that structural and dimensional changes can occur during conservation, and that some methods led to cracks in the wood structure [N1-F1]. The SEM comparison evidence in the hydrogel study states that SEM requires prior dehydration of the sample, which can alter the native structure and may affect the accuracy of microarchitecture observation [N5-F4]. This is directly relevant because the same principle applies to archaeological wood: sectioning and preparing a small fragment for SEM may preserve only a part of the original sample, while losing the larger context of how the wood was assembled, oriented, and altered during preservation [N5-F4]. The evidence does not provide explicit SEM-specific examples of orientation bias, but the general principle of sample preparation altering the apparent structure supports that conclusion [N4-F2][N5-F4].

In summary, the main preservation issues for degraded archaeological wood are: collapse and cracking from drying, heterogeneous degradation and resin loss, and post-depositional alteration that complicates interpretation; while sample size, orientation, and sectioning can further reduce representativeness [N4-F2][N1-F1][N5-F4].

Branch report on beam effects and imaging conditions

Beam energy, voltage, and dwell time cause beam-induced damage in SEM because the electron beam can permanently alter or degrade the sample over time. The general SEM beam-damage evidence states that the electron beam can permanently alter or degrade the sample that is being observed, and that beam damage is a physical limit and determines the resolution that can be achieved in imaging [N3-R4][N3-F3]. The organic-thin-film study shows that beam damage varies depending on parameters such as electron dose rate, temperature during imaging, and the presence of water and oxygen in the sample [N3-F3]. It also explains that beam damage occurs at different length scales and that the most important factor limiting acquisition of structural or chemical data at high spatial resolution is beam damage [N3-F3]. For organic materials, beam damage can include fading of diffraction spots and rings, mass loss, shrinkage, and changes in contrast or local intensity [N3-F3]. This means that even standard SEM imaging conditions can cause irreversible damage in fragile organic materials, especially when high voltage or long dwell times are used.

Charging and secondary electron yield affect image quality and artifact formation because non-conductive samples can build up electric charge, which distorts the image and creates artifacts. The SEM preparation evidence explains that conductive coatings are commonly applied to insulating or beam-sensitive materials to reduce electric charge buildup on the sample surface [N2-R3]. It also says that gold or platinum coating is used to reduce the charge that builds up on insulating samples, enabling sharp, high-resolution imaging [N2-R1][N2-R2]. This supports the idea that charging is a major imaging problem in non-conductive samples, but the evidence does not specifically link it to SEM artifacts in wood. Still, the general principle is that charging can reduce image quality by creating artifacts, and that conductive treatment is often used to mitigate that problem [N2-R3]. The beam-damage evidence also notes that many artifacts are a result of indirect electron beam interactions, such as production of reactive radicals in water by radiolysis [N3-R5]. This suggests that charging is only one of several artifact-generating mechanisms, and that secondary-electron yield and beam-induced reactions can together affect image quality.

Low-voltage imaging reduces damage but may degrade resolution or depth of field. The organic-thin-film study says that electron beam damage is affected by the temperature of the material, the electron flux through the material, and the accumulated amount of electrons transmitting the material [N3-F3]. It also states that beam damage constitutes a physical limit and determines the resolution that can be achieved in imaging [N3-F3]. While the evidence does not explicitly state that low voltage always improves resolution, it does support the general tradeoff: lower beam energy can reduce the dose and thus reduce damage, but it may also reduce the resolving power of the microscope [N3-R4][N3-F3]. The same evidence also notes that beam damage occurs at different length scales, which implies that low-voltage imaging may reduce some types of damage but not others, and that image quality can still be compromised by charging, sputtering, radiolysis, or other effects [N3-R4][N3-F3]. In practice, this means that low-voltage SEM can be used to preserve fragile samples, but users should expect lower resolution and possibly reduced depth of field compared to higher-voltage imaging [N3-R4][N3-F3].

Overall, the main beam effects are: beam energy/voltage and dwell time increase damage and reduce resolution; charging and secondary-electron interactions create artifacts; and low-voltage imaging can reduce damage but may degrade resolution or depth of field [N3-R4][N3-F3][N2-R3].

Branch report on alternative imaging approaches and their relevance to SEM limitations

Confocal and cryo-SEM compare with SEM in preserving structure and reducing artifacts, but each has trade-offs. The hydrogel comparison study states that SEM requires prior dehydration of the sample, which can alter the native structure and may affect the accuracy of microarchitecture observation [N5-F4]. It also notes that Cryo-SEM uses high-pressure cryofixation to vitrify the sample, preserving its structure in a near-native state; however, it is technically demanding and requires specialized equipment [N5-F4]. This suggests that Cryo-SEM is better suited to preserving the native structure of highly hydrated materials than SEM, but that it is not a simple replacement because of its complexity. Confocal microscopy is not directly compared in the provided evidence, but the broader SEM discussion indicates that non-SEM approaches are needed when dehydration alters the structure [N5-F4]. So, for fragile archaeological wood, Cryo-SEM may preserve structure better than SEM, but confocal approaches are not explicitly supported by the evidence here.

Cryo-FIB/SEM can mitigate beam damage but introduces its own workflow limitations. The cryo-FIB/SEM evidence says that cryogenic focused ion beam and scanning electron microscopy is used to reduce damage caused by ion and electron beams [N5-R5]. This is directly relevant because cryo-FIB/SEM is designed to minimize the damage that can occur during both ion beam milling and SEM imaging [N5-R5]. However, the evidence also says that artefacts can be introduced at any stage of the workflow in preparing and observing samples in cryo-SEM [N5-R4]. This means that while cryo-FIB/SEM can reduce beam-induced damage, it does not eliminate it, and the workflow itself can still produce artifacts. The evidence also implies that cryo-FIB/SEM is more complex and technically demanding than standard SEM, making it less practical for routine use [N5-R4][N5-R5].

What methods are better suited to fragile archaeological wood versus what SEM can still do? The evidence points to Cryo-SEM as better suited to preserving structure in highly hydrated materials because it can vitrify the sample and preserve the near-native state [N5-F4]. It also suggests that SEM can still be useful for imaging, but only if the sample is carefully prepared and if the beam conditions are chosen to minimize damage [N3-F3][N5-F4]. For fragile wood, the best balance may be a combination of cryogenic preservation and low-dose imaging rather than standard SEM under normal drying conditions [N3-F3][N5-F4]. The evidence also shows that SEM is still valuable when the sample is small enough to be prepared without major structural alteration, and when the material is not too beam-sensitive [N3-F3][N5-F4]. However, for highly sensitive, water-rich, or collapsed archaeological wood, the alternatives are more attractive because they preserve the native structure better [N5-F4].

In conclusion, Cryo-SEM is better at preserving structure and reducing artifacts than standard SEM, but it is technically demanding [N5-F4][N5-R4]. Cryo-FIB/SEM can reduce beam damage but introduces its own workflow limitations [N5-R4][N5-R5]. For fragile archaeological wood, cryogenic methods are better suited than SEM when preserving the native structure is the priority, while SEM can still be used when the sample is small, carefully prepared, and imaged under low-dose conditions [N5-F4][N3-F3].

Below, I synthesize those limitations into a single, evidence-based answer.

---

### 1) Sample preparation limitations

The most immediate limitation is that sample preparation for SEM often involves drying, dehydration, embalming, and mechanical handling, all of which can alter the original structure of the wood and create artifacts.
